title: What happens if you get struck by lightning?

lines.text: What happens if you get struck by lightning?
A bolt hotter than the sun's surface blows your shoes off.
Most of it skims your skin. Enough goes in to stop your heart.
Nobody touches you. They think you're electric. You're not.
One stranger starts CPR. That's what saves you.
You live, with a red fern scar. Nine in ten people do.
Ranger Roy Sullivan got struck seven times. He survived all seven.
You survived. Comment what stupid shenanigans Gary should try tomorrow.

experiment.ending: survives (absurd event usually played as death)
experiment.turn: myth-bust (not electric) -> CPR saves you -> Roy Sullivan 7 strikes
experiment.payoff: useful: lightning victims are safe to touch, start CPR
experiment.length: ~30 s (82 words; old scripts ran ~2.6 words/s)
facts: About 90% of people struck by lightning survive: US CDC / NOAA lightning safety
A lightning channel reaches ~30,000 K, about five times the sun's surface: NOAA National Weather Service
Flashover: most current passes over the skin surface; strikes can blow off shoes and clothing: Cooper, lightning injury reviews (Wilderness & Environmental Medicine)
Cardiac arrest from lightning: the heart often restarts but breathing does not; prompt CPR is life-saving; victims carry no charge: NWS lightning safety / American Heart Association
Lichtenberg (fern) figures fade within hours to days
Roy Sullivan, Shenandoah park ranger, struck 7 times 1942-1977: Guinness World Records
